options.a: Opening, maintaining, and supervising customer accounts and processing transactions
options.b: Reviewing and approving registration statements for new issues before SEC effectiveness
options.c: Recommending securities to retail customers and soliciting new brokerage accounts
options.d: Auditing the firm's annual financial statements as its independent accountant

distractorExplanations.b: Reviewing registration statements is an investment banking / SEC Corporation Finance function, not back-office operations work.
distractorExplanations.c: Recommending securities and soliciting accounts is a registered representative (Series 7) sales role, not an operations function.
distractorExplanations.d: An independent public accountant audits the firm's annual report under Rule 17a-5; operations staff are not the external auditor.

options.a: A signed trade confirmation from the customer, which substitutes for endorsement
options.b: Proper endorsement, registration match, and transfer procedures per industry rules
options.c: A notarized customer signature in place of a medallion signature guarantee
options.d: Delivery of a physical certificate, because book-entry positions are not good delivery

distractorExplanations.a: A trade confirmation documents the trade; it does not replace a proper endorsement or stock power for good delivery of certificates.
distractorExplanations.c: Transfer agents require a medallion signature guarantee for transfers; a notary acknowledgment is not an accepted substitute.
distractorExplanations.d: Most securities settle by book-entry at DTC; book-entry delivery is good delivery, so a physical certificate is not required.

options.a: Trade settles one calendar day after trade date
options.b: Trade settles two business days after trade date
options.c: Trade settles on the same business day as trade date
options.d: Trade settles one business day after trade date

distractorExplanations.a: Settlement counts business days, not calendar days; a Friday trade settles the following Monday, not Saturday.
distractorExplanations.b: Two business days (T+2) was the prior cycle; U.S. standard equity settlement moved to T+1 on May 28, 2024.
distractorExplanations.c: Same-day settlement (T+0, a 'cash' trade) is a special arrangement, not the standard regular-way settlement cycle.

options.a: Immediate free sale once deposited, since the plan already cleared it
options.b: Proper restriction coding, legend compliance, and release tracking
options.c: Transfer to the firm's DTC account as freely tradable street-name stock
options.d: Filing a Form 4 by the operations department on the customer's behalf

distractorExplanations.a: Depositing restricted stock does not lift the legend; removal needs issuer/counsel sign-off and Rule 144 conditions before sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Legended shares cannot be treated as freely tradable street-name stock until the issuer and transfer agent remove the restriction.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 4 is the insider's own Section 16 ownership report; filing it does not release a legend or establish ops restriction controls.

options.a: Orders priced at the NAV computed at the prior day's market close
options.b: Orders received after deadline also get that day's NAV
options.c: Orders received before fund deadline priced at that day's NAV
options.d: Orders priced at the intraday market price when the order executes

distractorExplanations.a: That is backward pricing; Rule 22c-1 requires forward pricing at the next NAV computed after the order is received.
distractorExplanations.b: Pricing after-deadline orders at that day's NAV is illegal late trading; those orders receive the next day's NAV.
distractorExplanations.d: Intraday execution pricing applies to ETFs and stocks; open-end mutual funds price once daily at the next computed NAV.

options.a: Collect elections from each holder before exchanging the target shares
options.b: Hold target positions unchanged until each customer submits certificates
options.c: Credit merger consideration on the record date set for shareholder voting
options.d: Exchange old shares for merger consideration per terms on payable date

distractorExplanations.a: Elections are collected for voluntary actions; a mandatory merger is applied to every holder without customer instructions.
distractorExplanations.b: Book-entry positions are exchanged through DTC on the effective/payable date; ops does not wait for customers to submit certificates.
distractorExplanations.c: The voting record date decides who may vote on the deal, not when consideration is paid; exchange occurs on the payable date.

options.a: Short sale without locate, insufficient securities, or counterparty fail
options.b: Customer entering a limit order rather than a market order on the sell
options.c: Customer selling long shares already held in the firm account in street name
options.d: A trade executed late in the day near the 4:00 p.m. market close

distractorExplanations.b: Order type affects execution price, not the seller's ability to deliver shares on settlement date, so it does not cause a fail.
distractorExplanations.c: Selling fully paid shares already held in street name is the normal way to ensure delivery; it does not cause a fail.
distractorExplanations.d: Execution time within the trading day does not affect delivery; the trade still settles T+1 from the firm's existing position.

options.a: Release funds once the check is endorsed and imaged on deposit
options.b: Hold funds per Regulation CC and firm policy until cleared
options.c: Hold funds for 30 calendar days on every check by SEC rule
options.d: Credit the account and permit withdrawal by wire the same day

distractorExplanations.a: Endorsement and imaging do not mean the check has cleared; funds stay on hold until collection to manage returned-check risk.
distractorExplanations.c: No SEC rule mandates a flat 30-day hold; hold periods follow firm policy and funds-availability schedules.
distractorExplanations.d: Same-day withdrawal of uncollected check funds is a classic check-kiting fraud path; holds apply until the check clears.

options.a: Only on the third business day after expiration through the OCC
options.b: Before expiration for European options whenever the holder chooses
options.c: On expiration for American options when holder exercises or is assigned
options.d: On expiration for every out-of-the-money option held in the customer account

distractorExplanations.a: OCC processes exercises on the exercise date with T+1 settlement; there is no three-day post-expiration processing window.
distractorExplanations.b: European-style options can be exercised only at expiration, so there is no early exercise or assignment to process.
distractorExplanations.d: OCC exercise-by-exception covers in-the-money contracts ($0.01 or more ITM); out-of-the-money options normally expire worthless.

options.a: Mailing confirmation to the new address only, then releasing pending wires
options.b: An updated W-9 and new CIP verification as if opening a new account
options.c: Suspension of trading in the account until the next quarterly statement
options.d: Verification procedures and possible hold on disbursements per fraud protocols

distractorExplanations.a: Confirming only at the new address lets a fraudster confirm their own change; notice should go to the prior address or contact on file.
distractorExplanations.b: An address change does not reopen the account; it triggers change verification and Red Flags review, not a full new CIP cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: Firms verify the change and may hold disbursements; freezing trading until the next statement cycle is not the required response.

options.a: Prime serves institutional clients with complex financing/custody needs
options.b: Prime serves retail clients who open margin accounts above $25,000
options.c: Prime settles trades on T+2 while retail accounts settle on T+1
options.d: Prime is exempt from Rule 15c3-3 customer protection requirements

distractorExplanations.b: Margin accounts above the $25,000 pattern-day-trader level are still retail; prime brokerage serves hedge funds and institutions.
distractorExplanations.c: Settlement cycle depends on the security, not the client type; prime and retail U.S. equity trades both settle T+1.
distractorExplanations.d: Prime brokerage customers' assets are still covered by Rule 15c3-3 possession/control and reserve formula requirements.

options.a: Market losses on securities when prices decline, within the same limits
options.b: Missing customer securities/cash if broker-dealer fails, within limits
options.c: Customer deposits in bank sweep accounts, up to $500,000 per customer
options.d: Losses from fraud by the customer's own investment adviser, within limits

distractorExplanations.a: SIPC restores missing customer property in a broker-dealer liquidation; it does not cover market losses from price declines.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash swept to a bank is covered by FDIC, not SIPC; SIPC's $500,000 limit (including $250,000 cash) applies to assets held at the broker-dealer.
distractorExplanations.d: SIPC does not insure against bad advice or adviser fraud outside a broker-dealer failure; it replaces missing assets in a liquidation.

options.a: Customer orders match the execution prices quoted on the NBBO at entry
options.b: Positions are reconciled monthly against customer account statements
options.c: Internal records match clearing firm, depositories, and general ledger
options.d: Cash balances reconcile to the bank, with positions reviewed at year-end

distractorExplanations.a: Comparing executions to the NBBO is a best-execution review, not the books-versus-street reconciliation done at end of day.
distractorExplanations.b: Reconciliation against depositories and the clearing firm is daily; a monthly statement comparison would let breaks age undetected.
distractorExplanations.d: Positions must be reconciled along with cash; deferring position breaks to year-end defeats prompt resolution and 17a-13 counts.

options.a: Written supervisory procedures for each office of supervisory jurisdiction
options.b: Copies of all customer complaints and their resolution for four years
options.c: Fingerprint records and Form U4 filings for associated persons
options.d: Customer account information including identity and contact details

distractorExplanations.a: Written supervisory procedures are required by FINRA Rule 3110, not by Rule 4512's customer account information rule.
distractorExplanations.b: Customer complaint records are FINRA Rule 4513 (four years); Rule 4512 covers account information such as name, residence, and trusted contact.
distractorExplanations.c: Fingerprinting is SEC Rule 17f-2 and Form U4 filing is FINRA registration under Rule 1010/1220; neither is Rule 4512.

options.a: Credit extended by brokers/dealers for securities purchases (margin)
options.b: Credit extended by banks for purchasing securities against collateral
options.c: Maintenance margin levels in margin accounts after the initial purchase
options.d: Borrowers' obligations when they obtain purpose credit from any lender

distractorExplanations.b: Bank loans secured by securities for buying securities fall under Regulation U, not Regulation T.
distractorExplanations.c: Maintenance margin is set by FINRA Rule 4210 and firm house rules; Reg T governs the initial extension of credit.
distractorExplanations.d: Regulation X applies the margin rules to borrowers obtaining purpose credit; Reg T applies to credit extended by broker-dealers.

options.a: Verification of identity only when a customer wires out funds
options.b: Collection of a government ID copy with no further verification
options.c: Reasonable procedures to verify identity when opening account
options.d: Filing each new customer's identity information with FinCEN

distractorExplanations.a: CIP verification is tied to account opening, not deferred until a withdrawal; outbound wires trigger fraud checks, not initial CIP.
distractorExplanations.b: Collecting ID alone is not enough; CIP requires risk-based procedures to verify the data by documentary or non-documentary methods.
distractorExplanations.d: CIP information is kept in the firm's own records for five years after account closing; it is not filed with FinCEN per customer.

options.a: Unsolicited orders placed by retail customers through a self-directed online brokerage account
options.b: Recommendations of securities to institutional customers by broker-dealers
options.c: Investment advice given by registered investment advisers to advisory clients
options.d: Recommendations of securities transactions and investment strategies to retail customers

distractorExplanations.a: Reg BI is triggered by a recommendation; unsolicited self-directed orders with no recommendation fall outside its care obligation.
distractorExplanations.b: Reg BI covers retail customers; recommendations to institutional accounts fall under FINRA Rule 2111 suitability instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Advisory clients of an RIA are covered by the Advisers Act fiduciary duty, not by Regulation Best Interest.

options.a: Municipal securities dealers and advisors
options.b: Issuers of municipal bonds and their disclosure
options.c: Corporate bond dealers reporting trades to TRACE
options.d: Banks underwriting U.S. Treasury securities

distractorExplanations.b: The MSRB has no direct authority over municipal issuers themselves; it regulates dealers and municipal advisors.
distractorExplanations.c: Corporate bond trade reporting to TRACE is a FINRA rule; MSRB trade reporting for munis runs through RTRS.
distractorExplanations.d: Treasury securities fall under the Government Securities Act and Treasury rules, not MSRB municipal regulation.

options.a: $2,000 in a margin account, the general minimum to buy on margin
options.b: $25,000 in margin account for day trading activity meeting definition
options.c: $50,000 in margin account once four day trades occur in five days
options.d: $100,000 in margin account for any customer making any day trade

distractorExplanations.a: $2,000 is the FINRA Rule 4210 minimum equity to open or maintain a margin account, not the higher pattern day trader threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: The PDT minimum is $25,000, not $50,000, although four or more day trades in five business days does trigger PDT status.
distractorExplanations.d: PDT status needs four or more day trades in five business days (over 6% of trades), and the minimum equity is $25,000, not $100,000.

options.a: Market makers charging brokers access fees for executing marketable orders
options.b: Broker paying research providers with client commissions under soft-dollar terms
options.c: Broker internalizing orders as principal, which removes best execution duties
options.d: Broker routing equity orders to venues that pay for flow with best execution obligations

distractorExplanations.a: Access fees run from the broker to the venue; PFOF is the reverse, compensation paid to the broker for routing orders.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes soft-dollar arrangements under Exchange Act Section 28(e), not payment for order flow from market makers.
distractorExplanations.c: Internalized orders still carry best-execution obligations under FINRA Rule 5310; internalization does not remove that duty.

options.a: Failures to deliver in short sale positions
options.b: Locates obtained before effecting short sales
options.c: Marking sell orders as long or short at entry
options.d: Short sale price tests after a 10% price decline

distractorExplanations.b: The locate is a Reg SHO Rule 203(b)(1) pre-trade requirement; Rule 204 close-out addresses fails after settlement date.
distractorExplanations.c: Order marking is Reg SHO Rule 200(g); close-out under Rule 204 addresses fails to deliver after settlement date.
distractorExplanations.d: The 10% circuit-breaker price test is Rule 201 (alternative uptick rule), not the Rule 204 close-out requirement.

options.a: Screen customers against OFAC lists at account opening, then annually
options.b: Screen customers and transactions against blocked persons/country lists
options.c: File a Suspicious Activity Report with FinCEN within 30 days of a match
options.d: Obtain OFAC approval before opening any account for a non-U.S. citizen

distractorExplanations.a: OFAC screening is ongoing: new transactions and list updates must be screened, not just an annual re-check after onboarding.
distractorExplanations.c: OFAC matches are blocked or rejected and reported to OFAC within 10 business days; SARs to FinCEN are a separate BSA process.
distractorExplanations.d: OFAC does not pre-approve foreign customers; firms screen names against the SDN and sanctions lists and block only true matches.

options.a: Retention of business emails for three years with no format requirement
options.b: Retention of business emails for six years in any rewriteable format
options.c: WORM/non-rewriteable format for specified communications retention
options.d: Retention of personal-device business texts at the employee's discretion

distractorExplanations.a: 17a-4 sets both the period (generally three years, first two easily accessible) and the format (WORM or audit-trail), so no-format is wrong.
distractorExplanations.b: Communications are generally kept three years under 17a-4(b)(4), and electronic storage must be WORM or audit-trail, not rewriteable.
distractorExplanations.d: Business communications on personal devices must be captured by the firm; leaving it to employees is the off-channel failure the SEC fined.

options.a: Cash bonuses the firm pays associated persons above $100 per year
options.b: Business entertainment such as meals hosted with the client present
options.c: Gifts to a customer's family members for personal life events such as weddings
options.d: Non-cash gifts from vendors to associated persons beyond de minimis thresholds

distractorExplanations.a: Firm compensation to its own employees is not a gift under Rule 3220, which addresses gifts relating to another employer's business.
distractorExplanations.b: Business entertainment where the host attends is not subject to the Rule 3220 gift limit; it is governed by firm entertainment policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Personal gifts for life events such as weddings are excluded from the 3220 limit when not given in relation to the recipient employer's business.

options.a: Firm ops/proxy department forwarding materials and processing instructions per policy
options.b: The transfer agent mailing proxies directly to each street-name beneficial owner
options.c: The issuer voting street-name shares in line with management recommendations
options.d: The DTC voting all street-name shares as the nominee holder of record

distractorExplanations.b: Transfer agents mail to registered holders; street-name owners receive materials through their broker or its agent such as Broadridge.
distractorExplanations.c: Issuers cannot vote shares they do not own; street-name shares are voted on the beneficial owner's instruction or broker routine discretion.
distractorExplanations.d: DTC passes voting authority to its participants through an omnibus proxy; it does not itself vote beneficial owners' shares.

options.a: Trade on information only after it appears in a firm research note
options.b: Possess material nonpublic information from firm processing activities
options.c: Trade in their own accounts at an outside broker without pre-clearance
options.d: Execute customer orders without exercising any investment discretion

distractorExplanations.a: Trading after publication in research uses public information; the prohibition covers trading on MNPI before public dissemination.
distractorExplanations.c: Trading away without pre-clearance breaks firm policy and Rule 3210 consent rules, but insider-trading law turns on possessing MNPI.
distractorExplanations.d: Executing nondiscretionary orders is routine processing and not itself insider trading; liability turns on trading while holding MNPI.

options.a: Debit customer payable/liability, credit cash/asset
options.b: Debit cash/asset, credit customer receivable/asset
options.c: Debit cash/asset, credit customer payable/liability
options.d: Debit cash/asset, credit commission revenue/income

distractorExplanations.a: This reverses the entry: a deposit increases the cash asset (debit) and the amount owed to the customer (credit).
distractorExplanations.b: A customer receivable is a debit balance the customer owes; deposited cash is owed back to the customer, so it is a payable.
distractorExplanations.d: Customer cash is not earned revenue; it is a liability to the customer until fees are actually charged to the account.

options.a: Positions and balances, with trade activity shown on confirms instead
options.b: Activity for the period, with holdings shown only once a year
options.c: Balances and fees, with positions reported on the annual Form 1099
options.d: Positions, balances, activity, and fees for the period accurately

distractorExplanations.a: Confirms do not replace statement activity; FINRA Rule 2231 statements must show securities positions, money balances, and account activity.
distractorExplanations.b: Statements must show positions every period (at least quarterly under Rule 2231), not once a year.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 1099 is a tax report of income and sales; it does not substitute for the positions section of a periodic account statement.

options.a: Customer funds held in escrow until a trade settles
options.b: Transactions pending identification or resolution
options.c: Firm proprietary positions awaiting a sale decision
options.d: Dormant balances awaiting escheatment to the state

distractorExplanations.a: Unsettled trade money sits in customer and settlement accounts, not suspense; suspense is for items that cannot yet be identified.
distractorExplanations.c: Proprietary inventory sits in firm trading accounts; suspense holds unidentified or unresolved items pending correct booking.
distractorExplanations.d: Dormant balances stay in the customer's account until escheated; suspense is a temporary holding area for unresolved items.

options.a: A weekly reserve computation covering customer fully paid securities
options.b: Pledging fully paid securities up to 140% of the customer's debit balance
options.c: Possession or control procedures protecting customer securities
options.d: Annual physical counts of customer securities under Rule 17a-13

distractorExplanations.a: The weekly reserve formula protects customer cash credits; fully paid securities are protected by possession or control, not the reserve deposit.
distractorExplanations.b: The 140% hypothecation limit applies to margin securities; fully paid securities may not be pledged and must be kept in possession or control.
distractorExplanations.d: Rule 17a-13 box counts are quarterly, not annual, and are a separate control; 15c3-3 protection works through possession or control.

options.a: Order details and execution prices, retained for one year under 17a-4
options.b: Customer names, addresses, and investment objectives for each account
options.c: Supervisory approvals of new accounts and their documentation dates
options.d: Order details, timestamps, execution prices, and account identifiers

distractorExplanations.a: Blotters are 17a-3(a)(1) records kept six years under 17a-4(a), the first two in an easily accessible place, not one year.
distractorExplanations.b: Customer name, address, and objective data belong in the account record under 17a-3(a)(17) and Rule 4512, not the trade blotter.
distractorExplanations.c: New-account approvals are account-opening records, not blotter entries of daily purchases, sales, receipts, and deliveries.

options.a: Transferring remaining cash after securities moved per customer request
options.b: Sweeping remaining cash to the firm's error account pending research
options.c: Transferring remaining margin debit balances to the receiving firm later
options.d: Mailing a check for remaining cash to the customer's address of record

distractorExplanations.b: Residual credits belong to the customer and are forwarded through the ACATS residual process, not parked in an error account.
distractorExplanations.c: Residual credit means money owed to the customer (cash, dividends, interest), not a margin debit owed by the customer.
distractorExplanations.d: Under FINRA Rule 11870, residual credits after a full transfer are sent to the receiving firm through ACATS, not mailed to the customer.

options.a: Gain recognition when substantially identical security repurchased within 30 days
options.b: Loss deduction when substantially identical security repurchased within 30 days
options.c: Loss deduction when a security in the same sector is repurchased within 30 days
options.d: Loss deduction when substantially identical security repurchased within 60 days

distractorExplanations.a: The wash sale rule disallows losses only; gains on a sale followed by a repurchase are recognized normally.
distractorExplanations.c: Only substantially identical securities trigger a wash sale; buying a different company in the same sector does not.
distractorExplanations.d: The window is 30 days before or after the sale (a 61-day period), not 60 days after the sale.

options.a: Remitting unclaimed property to the SEC once the statutory dormancy period lapses
options.b: Remitting unclaimed property to the state of the firm's headquarters
options.c: Reporting and remitting unclaimed property to state after dormancy period
options.d: Transferring dormant accounts to SIPC after a dormancy period lapses

distractorExplanations.a: Unclaimed property is escheated to the states under state law, not to the SEC.
distractorExplanations.b: Priority rules send property to the state of the owner's last known address first; the firm's domicile state is only the fallback.
distractorExplanations.d: SIPC protects customers in broker-dealer liquidations; it does not take custody of dormant accounts or unclaimed property.

options.a: Last shares purchased are first shares sold for gain/loss calculation
options.b: Highest-cost shares are first shares sold for gain/loss calculation
options.c: Average cost per share of the position is used for gain/loss calculation
options.d: First shares purchased are first shares sold for gain/loss calculation

distractorExplanations.a: Last-in, first-out is LIFO; FIFO relieves the earliest acquired lots first.
distractorExplanations.b: Highest-cost-first is HIFO, a tax-lot election the customer can choose, not FIFO.
distractorExplanations.c: Average cost is a separate method common for mutual fund shares; FIFO matches the earliest lots, not a blended cost.

options.a: Interest charged on the client's margin debit balance under the financing terms
options.b: Costs associated with securities borrowing/lending or settlement fails per agreement
options.c: Penalties FINRA assesses on the client for late Reg SHO close-outs on short sales
options.d: Custody fees for safekeeping fully paid securities held in segregation

distractorExplanations.a: Margin interest is a financing charge on the debit balance, shown separately from borrow or settlement fail charges.
distractorExplanations.c: Reg SHO close-out duties fall on the clearing participant, and FINRA does not post fines to client statements as fail charges.
distractorExplanations.d: Custody or safekeeping fees are a service charge on held assets, not a cost arising from borrow or settlement fails.

options.a: Produce records within 30 days of a written request
options.b: Produce records only after counsel reviews them first
options.c: Produce required records promptly and accurately
options.d: Produce summaries in place of the underlying records

distractorExplanations.a: Records must be produced promptly on request under 17a-4(j) and Rule 8210; there is no 30-day grace period for examiners.
distractorExplanations.b: Firms may involve counsel, but production to examiners cannot be held back pending legal review; prompt production is required.
distractorExplanations.d: Examiners can require the actual books and records, not firm-prepared summaries, under Rule 8210 and 17a-4(j).

options.a: Cash owed by the customer on a margin debit balance
options.b: Cash in the customer's account pledged as collateral
options.c: Cash swept to an FDIC-insured bank deposit program
options.d: Cash payable to customer on demand subject to holds

distractorExplanations.a: A margin debit is money the customer owes the firm; a free credit balance is money the firm owes the customer.
distractorExplanations.b: Cash pledged against a short or margin position is not free; free credits are unencumbered and payable on demand.
distractorExplanations.c: Swept bank deposits are held at a bank, not at the broker-dealer as a free credit balance under Rule 15c3-3.

options.a: Firm will receive and pass through dividend to entitled accounts
options.b: Dividends credit to accounts that bought on or after the ex-date
options.c: Dividends credit to accounts holding on the declaration date
options.d: Dividends post to accounts on the record date, ahead of payment

distractorExplanations.b: Buyers on or after the ex-date are not entitled; under T+1 the ex-date and record date fall on the same day.
distractorExplanations.c: Entitlement is set by holdings at the record date, not on the declaration date when the board announces the dividend.
distractorExplanations.d: The record date fixes entitlement; cash is not credited until the issuer pays on the payable date.

options.a: Price declines in the firm's proprietary inventory positions
options.b: Failed processes, systems outages, fraud, and human error
options.c: Counterparty default on unsecured lending and margin debits
options.d: Inability to fund settlements because cash is tied up

distractorExplanations.a: Price movements in firm inventory are market risk, a separate category from operational risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Losses from a borrower or counterparty failing to pay are credit risk, not operational risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Being unable to meet funding obligations is liquidity risk; operational risk stems from processes, people, and systems.

options.a: A customer adding a trusted contact person to the account profile
options.b: Repeated small dividend reinvestments posted over several months
options.c: Password reset, new bank link, and large wire to new payee same day
options.d: A long-time customer requesting paper statements after years of e-delivery

distractorExplanations.a: Adding a trusted contact under FINRA Rule 4512 is a protective step, not an account takeover red flag by itself.
distractorExplanations.b: Routine dividend reinvestment is expected account activity and does not signal credential compromise.
distractorExplanations.d: Switching delivery preference is a minor service change; takeover patterns combine credential changes with outbound funds.

options.a: Sign off on each report once the exception count is below target
options.b: Review exceptions quarterly when preparing the annual 3130 certification
options.c: Reassign aged items to the staff member who created each break
options.d: Verify timely resolution and escalate unresolved aged items

distractorExplanations.a: A low count is not proof of resolution; supervisors must check that each item is resolved and escalate aged ones.
distractorExplanations.b: Exception reports need ongoing review; waiting for the Rule 3130 CEO certification cycle lets breaks age.
distractorExplanations.c: Routing breaks back to their originator weakens segregation of duties and is not escalation to supervision.

options.a: Alternate site, data backup, staffing, and communication during disruption
options.b: Alternate site and data backup, with plan review every five years
options.c: Data backup and recovery, with customer access deferred until restored
options.d: Recovery steps filed with the SEC for approval before implementation

distractorExplanations.b: Rule 4370 requires the plan to be updated for material changes and reviewed annually, not every five years.
distractorExplanations.c: Rule 4370 requires the plan to address how customers get prompt access to funds and securities during a disruption.
distractorExplanations.d: Firms keep BCPs internally and report emergency contacts to FINRA; plans are not filed with the SEC for approval.

options.a: Account equity rises above requirements, creating excess SMA for the customer
options.b: Account equity falls below requirements and customer fails to meet calls
options.c: Customer pays for a cash account purchase within the Reg T payment period
options.d: Customer deposits fully paid securities that the firm keeps in segregation

distractorExplanations.a: Rising equity creates SMA (buying power), which reduces rather than creates credit risk for the firm.
distractorExplanations.c: Timely payment in a cash account means no credit exposure; risk arises from margin debits that are not met.
distractorExplanations.d: Segregated fully paid securities carry no loan, so there is no customer credit exposure to the firm.

options.a: Customer margin securities pledged to banks under hypothecation
options.b: Customer free credit balances held in the reserve bank account
options.c: Proprietary trading desk holdings subject to price changes
options.d: Customer fully paid securities held in the firm's DTC account

distractorExplanations.a: Hypothecated customer collateral remains customer property; its price risk sits with the customer, not firm inventory.
distractorExplanations.b: Reserve account deposits protect customer cash; they are not firm inventory exposed to market price changes.
distractorExplanations.d: Segregated customer securities belong to customers; their price changes are not firm proprietary market risk.

options.a: Update the record to the newest address and process pending wires
options.b: File a Suspicious Activity Report before contacting the customer
options.c: Close the account and return assets to the address on the latest form
options.d: Trigger enhanced due diligence and hold on disbursements pending resolution

distractorExplanations.a: Accepting the newest data without verification is how account takeovers succeed; resolve the conflict before releasing funds.
distractorExplanations.b: A mismatch alone is a red flag to investigate; a SAR follows if the review finds suspicious activity, not as a first step.
distractorExplanations.c: Closing and sending assets to an unverified address compounds the fraud risk; investigate and hold disbursements first.

options.a: Temporary placement of trade errors until allocated correctly
options.b: Holding unallocated block trades until advisers send allocations
options.c: Absorbing customer losses on trades the customer later regrets
options.d: Parking unidentified cash receipts until the payer is confirmed

distractorExplanations.b: Unallocated blocks belong in an average-price or allocation account, not the error account.
distractorExplanations.c: Customer-directed trades the customer regrets are not firm errors; moving them to the error account is improper.
distractorExplanations.d: Unidentified receipts go to a suspense account; the error account is reserved for trade errors.

options.a: Longer settlement cycles that give firms more time to match trades
options.b: Shorter settlement cycles and central clearing (T+1, CCP)
options.c: Bilateral netting with each counterparty instead of a central CCP
options.d: Free delivery of securities before payment is received

distractorExplanations.a: Longer cycles increase exposure between trade and settlement; T+1 shortened the window to cut risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Bilateral netting leaves counterparty exposure in place; central clearing through a CCP such as NSCC is the stronger mitigant.
distractorExplanations.d: Free delivery is the textbook source of Herstatt risk; DVP and PvP link delivery to payment to remove it.

options.a: Broad system access for senior staff so they can cover absences
options.b: Dual control over outbound wires, with reconciliation done by the wire initiator
options.c: Least privilege access, logging, segregation of duties, and background checks
options.d: Annual background checks, with access reviews left to the IT vendor

distractorExplanations.a: Broad access violates least privilege; absence coverage should use role-based backups with logging.
distractorExplanations.b: Letting the wire initiator also reconcile defeats segregation of duties; reconciliation must be independent.
distractorExplanations.d: Access recertification is a firm control that cannot be outsourced away; background checks alone do not mitigate insider threat.

options.a: Determine which complaints must be reported under Rule 4530
options.b: Calculate customer restitution owed on each individual complaint
options.c: Set staff incentive pay based on complaint counts per employee
options.d: Identify systematic process failures requiring remediation

distractorExplanations.a: 4530 reporting is decided complaint by complaint; trending is for spotting systemic causes across many complaints.
distractorExplanations.b: Restitution is decided case by case; trend analysis looks for repeated root causes across complaints.
distractorExplanations.c: Tying pay to complaint counts discourages logging complaints; trending is meant to find process failures.

options.a: Best execution and liability exposure requiring prompt correction
options.b: A Reg SHO close-out obligation by the start of trading on T+2
options.c: Exposure only if the customer files a written complaint first
options.d: A trade reporting violation to be fixed at month-end reconciliation

distractorExplanations.b: Reg SHO close-outs address fails to deliver on short sales, not unfilled customer limit orders.
distractorExplanations.c: The firm's duty to correct the error and make the customer whole exists whether or not the customer complains.
distractorExplanations.d: The issue is execution quality and customer harm, and it needs prompt correction, not month-end cleanup.

options.a: Quarterly revenue per registered representative and new account growth
options.b: Aged fail percentage, break rate, and STP straight-through processing rate
options.c: Firm net capital ratio and the size of its proprietary inventory
options.d: Average client portfolio return compared with its stated benchmark

distractorExplanations.a: Revenue and account growth are business performance metrics, not indicators of operational control risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Net capital and inventory size measure financial and market risk, not operational process health.
distractorExplanations.d: Portfolio performance measures investment results, not the operational failure rate a KRI tracks.

options.a: Reliance on the vendor's SOC 2 report in place of oversight
options.b: A vendor indemnity clause that transfers regulatory liability
options.c: Due diligence, contract SLAs, and ongoing monitoring
options.d: Due diligence at onboarding, with renewal reviews every 5 years

distractorExplanations.a: A SOC report is one input; FINRA Regulatory Notice 21-29 says the firm keeps supervisory responsibility for outsourced functions.
distractorExplanations.b: Contracts cannot transfer a member firm's regulatory obligations; the firm remains responsible for outsourced activities.
distractorExplanations.d: Vendor oversight must be ongoing and risk-based, not a one-time onboarding check revisited every five years.

options.a: Only specified assets the customer designates, leaving other holdings at the delivering firm
options.b: Every asset in the account, with the delivering firm closing it after settlement
options.c: Specified assets, but processed outside ACATS as a manual DTC free delivery
options.d: Specified assets once the delivering firm validates the request within five business days

distractorExplanations.b: Moving every asset and closing the account is a full transfer; a partial transfer leaves non-designated holdings behind.
distractorExplanations.c: Partial transfers are a supported ACATS transaction type; they do not need to be handled as manual free deliveries.
distractorExplanations.d: Under FINRA Rule 11870 the delivering firm must validate or take exception within one business day, not five.

options.a: Apply the default option to each holder on the effective date without notice
options.b: Notify customers and accept elections up to the payable date set by the issuer
options.c: Notify customers, collect elections by deadline, and submit instructions
options.d: Tender shares for each holder and let customers withdraw before the offer expires

distractorExplanations.a: Defaults apply only when a holder does not respond after notice; a voluntary offer requires notifying holders and collecting elections first.
distractorExplanations.b: Elections must arrive before the firm's internal deadline ahead of offer expiration; the payable date comes after the offer closes.
distractorExplanations.d: The firm cannot tender without instructions; in a voluntary offer customers opt in rather than being tendered and opting out.

series-99-readiness-check-ops-019.explanation: Voluntary actions require timely client communication and accurate election processing. Instructions are submitted to the issuer's tender or exchange agent.

options.a: Legend removal by the firm's own operations team once the shares are deposited
options.b: Holding the shares for one year before any sale, as Rule 144 requires
options.c: Filing Form 144 for any sale, even when shares are freely tradable
options.d: Restriction legend tracking, release schedules, and compliance with Rule 144

distractorExplanations.a: The issuer's transfer agent removes a legend, typically after an issuer or counsel opinion; the firm's ops team cannot remove it.
distractorExplanations.b: For an SEC-reporting issuer the Rule 144 holding period is six months; one year applies to non-reporting issuers, so a blanket hold is wrong.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 144 is needed for affiliate or restricted sales above 5,000 shares or $50,000 in three months, not for any freely tradable sale.

series-99-readiness-check-ops-020.explanation: Ops tracks control restrictions and release dates before unrestricted trading. Rule 144 compliance applies where the shares are restricted or held by an affiliate.

options.a: Verify authorization, confirm payee details, and apply fraud controls per firm policy
options.b: Confirm the request by email reply to the address on file, then release
options.c: Verify authorization only for wires to third parties, not to the customer's bank
options.d: Release the wire and complete identity verification after it settles

distractorExplanations.b: Email confirmation can be intercepted by a fraudster who controls the mailbox; a callback to a phone number on file is the standard.
distractorExplanations.c: First-party wires to a newly linked bank are a top takeover path; authorization and payee checks apply to first-party wires too.
distractorExplanations.d: Verification after release is too late; wired funds are hard to recall, so controls must run before release.

options.a: Collect customer elections before crediting cash on payment date
options.b: Remove target shares and credit cash proceeds on payment date
options.c: Credit cash proceeds on the record date and remove shares at payment
options.d: Remove target shares and credit acquirer stock at the exchange ratio

distractorExplanations.a: Elections are for voluntary or cash/stock election deals; a mandatory cash merger is processed for every holder without instructions.
distractorExplanations.c: In a cash merger, shares are removed and cash credited together on payment date; the record date does not trigger the cash credit.
distractorExplanations.d: Crediting acquirer stock describes a stock-for-stock merger; a cash merger pays a fixed cash amount per share.

series-99-readiness-check-ops-022.explanation: Mandatory mergers exchange shares for cash and/or acquirer stock per terms on effective date. Corporate action entries are posted to each account on the payment date.

options.a: Customer selling long shares held at the firm in fully paid street name
options.b: Customer buying shares on margin instead of paying in full by T+1
options.c: Short seller lacking locate/borrow or deliverer missing shares at settlement
options.d: Short seller obtaining a locate and borrowing shares before settlement

distractorExplanations.a: Long sales from fully paid street-name positions are deliverable from the firm's DTC account and do not cause fails.
distractorExplanations.b: Margin purchases are financed by the firm and settle normally; how a buyer pays does not create a fail to deliver.
distractorExplanations.d: A locate plus a borrow before settlement lets the seller deliver; that prevents rather than causes a fail.

options.a: Make check funds available for trading and withdrawal the next business day
options.b: Apply a fixed 10-business-day hold set by FINRA to every check deposit
options.c: Hold funds for trading but permit wires out of the account immediately
options.d: Apply hold periods per firm policy and applicable funds-availability rules

distractorExplanations.a: Next-day availability for withdrawals invites returned-check fraud; firms hold funds per policy until the check is collected.
distractorExplanations.b: FINRA sets no uniform check-hold period; hold schedules come from firm policy informed by funds-availability rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Wiring out uncollected funds is the highest-risk release; restricting trading but not withdrawals inverts the control.

series-99-readiness-check-ops-024.explanation: Broker-dealers apply hold schedules and fraud controls on check deposits; bank-like Reg CC schedules may inform policy but the firm’s procedures govern release for trading. Holds apply before funds are released for trading.

options.a: On any business day the long holder exercises, including before expiration
options.b: Only on expiration day, since early exercise applies to European options
options.c: On the day OCC receives exercise notice, with assignment deferred to expiry
options.d: At expiration for any contract in the money by at least $1.00

distractorExplanations.b: That reverses the styles: American options allow early exercise, while European options are exercisable only at expiration.
distractorExplanations.c: OCC assigns exercise notices to clearing members on the exercise date itself; assignment is not deferred to expiration.
distractorExplanations.d: OCC exercise by exception applies at $0.01 in the money, and early exercise can trigger assignment before expiration anyway.

options.a: Updated mailings to the new address, with disbursements processed as usual
options.b: Verification procedures, possible hold on disbursements, and updated mailings
options.c: A new account form and fresh CIP verification as if opening the account
options.d: Notice to FINRA through an amended Form U4 within 30 days of the change

distractorExplanations.a: Disbursements right after an address change are a classic takeover pattern; firms verify and may hold them first.
distractorExplanations.c: An address change does not restart CIP; it triggers change verification and identity-theft red flags review.
distractorExplanations.d: Form U4 covers registered persons' information; customer address changes are internal account records under Rule 4512.

series-99-readiness-check-ops-026.explanation: Address changes are common fraud vectors; firms verify identity before releasing assets. This follows the firm's AML and identity-theft red flags policy.

options.a: Mutual fund breakpoint tracking and 529 plan account servicing
options.b: Cash-account trading settled delivery versus payment at a custodian
options.c: Securities lending, margin financing, and consolidated reporting
options.d: Odd-lot dividend reinvestment and paper certificate safekeeping

distractorExplanations.a: Breakpoints and 529 plans are retail product servicing needs, not hedge fund financing and custody services.
distractorExplanations.b: DVP/RVP accounts settle at an outside custodian without financing; prime clients need leverage, borrows, and consolidated reporting.
distractorExplanations.d: DRIP and certificate safekeeping are retail services; prime brokerage centers on financing, securities lending, and reporting.

series-99-readiness-check-ops-027.explanation: Prime services support hedge funds and institutions with complex financing and reporting. Capital introduction is another common prime brokerage service.

options.a: Verify ex-date trades and file a claim with the issuer's transfer agent
options.b: Verify declaration date holdings and credit the dividend if shares were held
options.c: Issue a goodwill credit for the dividend and research the break afterward
options.d: Verify record date holdings, payment date entries, and entitlements on the account

distractorExplanations.a: Claims go to the counterparty or through DTC after research; the first step is reconciling the account's record date entitlement.
distractorExplanations.b: Entitlement depends on record date holdings, not on what the customer held on the declaration date.
distractorExplanations.c: Crediting before research risks a duplicate payment; ops must first confirm entitlement and posting.

options.a: Shares credit on settlement date with correct restricted status and cost basis
options.b: Shares credit on trade date at the first-day closing price as cost basis
options.c: Shares credit to restricted persons under Rule 5130 like other customers
options.d: Shares credit after the 25-day quiet period ends for each allocated account

distractorExplanations.b: IPO cost basis is the public offering price, and shares post on settlement date, not at the first-day close on trade date.
distractorExplanations.c: Rule 5130 bars allocating new issues to restricted persons such as broker-dealer personnel; ops must exclude them.
distractorExplanations.d: The research quiet period limits analyst reports; it does not delay settlement of allocated IPO shares.

series-99-readiness-check-ops-029.explanation: Allocations must reflect offering price, restrictions, and settlement through standard channels. This applies to each allocated customer account.

options.a: U.S. settlement cycles applied to every market, with local holidays noted
options.b: Local market settlement cycles, holiday calendars, and currency cut-off times
options.c: Holiday calendars of the trade's home market, with FX settled on the trade date
options.d: Currency cut-off times in New York, since all FX settles through CHIPS

distractorExplanations.a: Many foreign markets settle T+2 or on other cycles; applying the U.S. T+1 cycle everywhere causes cross-border fails.
distractorExplanations.c: Settlement needs both markets' calendars and FX funding within currency cut-offs (spot FX is T+2), not same-day FX on one calendar.
distractorExplanations.d: FX settles in each currency's home payment system (CLS, local RTGS), so desks track local cut-offs, not just New York CHIPS.

series-99-readiness-check-ops-030.explanation: Cross-border ops aligns settlement dates and FX funding across jurisdictions. These matter most for cross-border trades.

options.a: Paper or electronic form, kept for three years when no other period is specified
options.b: Electronic form only, with paper records converted within one year
options.c: Any format the firm chooses, provided it keeps records for two years
options.d: A format that is readily accessible and auditable for required retention periods

distractorExplanations.a: Rule 4511(b) sets a six-year default for records with no specified period under FINRA rules or 17a-4, not three years.
distractorExplanations.b: Rule 4511 and 17a-4 permit paper or compliant electronic records; there is no mandatory one-year paper conversion.
distractorExplanations.c: Records must be kept in a 17a-4-compliant format under 4511(c), and the default retention under 4511(b) is six years, not two.

options.a: Business continuity and contingency plans for critical operations
options.b: Written supervisory procedures for each office of supervisory jurisdiction
options.c: Annual CEO certification of compliance and supervisory processes
options.d: Customer account information records including a trusted contact

distractorExplanations.b: Written supervisory procedures are required by Rule 3110; Rule 4370 is the business continuity plan rule.
distractorExplanations.c: The annual CEO certification is Rule 3130; Rule 4370 covers business continuity plans and emergency contacts.
distractorExplanations.d: Account information and trusted contact persons are FINRA Rule 4512, not the Rule 4370 business continuity rule.

options.a: File Currency Transaction Reports for cash deposits of $3,000 or more in a day
options.b: Implement AML programs including customer due diligence and suspicious activity monitoring
options.c: File Suspicious Activity Reports with FINRA for any suspicious transaction of $2,000 or more
options.d: Implement AML programs reviewed by an independent tester every five years

distractorExplanations.a: CTRs are filed for cash over $10,000 in a business day; $3,000 is the monetary instrument purchase recordkeeping threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: SARs are filed with FinCEN, not FINRA, and the broker-dealer threshold is $5,000; $2,000 is the money services business threshold.
distractorExplanations.d: FINRA Rule 3310 requires independent AML testing annually (every two years for certain firms), not every five years.

options.a: Verify identity of customers using documentary methods, as non-documentary ones are barred
options.b: Verify identity of customers by obtaining each customer's Social Security card copy
options.c: Verify identity of customers opening accounts using documentary or non-documentary methods
options.d: Verify identity of account owners and file the CIP records with FinCEN each month

distractorExplanations.a: The CIP rule expressly allows non-documentary methods such as credit bureau checks, alone or combined with documents.
distractorExplanations.b: CIP does not require an SSN card; it requires a taxpayer ID number and risk-based verification by documents or other means.
distractorExplanations.d: CIP records are kept by the firm for five years after the account closes; they are not filed with FinCEN.

options.a: Broker-dealer recommendations of securities and accounts to institutional customers
options.b: Investment adviser recommendations to advisory clients under the Advisers Act
options.c: Broker-dealer execution of unsolicited orders for retail self-directed accounts
options.d: Broker-dealer recommendations of securities and accounts to retail customers

distractorExplanations.a: Reg BI covers retail customers; institutional recommendations remain under FINRA Rule 2111 suitability.
distractorExplanations.b: RIAs owe a fiduciary duty under the Advisers Act; Reg BI applies to broker-dealers and their associated persons.
distractorExplanations.c: Reg BI is triggered by a recommendation; unsolicited self-directed orders without a recommendation are outside it.

options.a: Broker-dealers and municipal advisors engaged in municipal securities activities
options.b: State and local issuers that sell municipal bonds to fund public projects
options.c: Broker-dealers trading corporate bonds and reporting those trades to TRACE
options.d: Banks and dealers in U.S. Treasury securities under the Government Securities Act

distractorExplanations.b: The MSRB cannot regulate municipal issuers directly; issuer disclosure is reached through dealer rules such as SEC Rule 15c2-12.
distractorExplanations.c: Corporate bond dealing and TRACE reporting are FINRA rules; MSRB rules govern municipal securities activities.
distractorExplanations.d: Treasury dealers are regulated under the Government Securities Act by Treasury, the SEC, and bank regulators, not the MSRB.

options.a: $2,000 in the margin account, the same minimum required to open any margin account
options.b: $25,000 in the margin account before day trading is permitted without restriction
options.c: $50,000 in the margin account, of which half may be met with a customer's cash account
options.d: $100,000 in the margin account, with day trading buying power limited to 2x equity

distractorExplanations.a: $2,000 is the Rule 4210 minimum equity for a margin account; pattern day traders need $25,000.
distractorExplanations.c: PDT minimum equity is $25,000 and must be held in the margin account; cash-account balances do not count toward it.
distractorExplanations.d: The PDT minimum is $25,000, and day-trading buying power is up to 4x maintenance margin excess, not 2x equity.

options.a: Complaints are made orally or in writing, once three are received from one customer
options.b: Complaints involve service delays and are not resolved within 30 days of receipt
options.c: Complaints involve allegations of theft, misappropriation, or certain sales practice violations
options.d: Complaints allege customer losses above $5,000, with the report due to FINRA within 90 days

distractorExplanations.a: 4530 reporting concerns written customer complaints; there is no three-complaints-per-customer trigger.
distractorExplanations.b: Service delays are not a 4530(a) trigger; 30 days is the deadline to report a specified event, not a complaint test.
distractorExplanations.d: 4530(a) events are reported within 30 days, and complaint reporting turns on the allegation type (theft, misappropriation, forgery), not a dollar amount.

options.a: The firm pays market makers a fee to execute orders at the NBBO midpoint
options.b: The customer's orders will be routed to the venue paying the highest rebate
options.c: The firm receives commissions from customers for each order it routes
options.d: The firm may receive compensation from market makers for routing orders

distractorExplanations.a: PFOF flows from market makers to the broker, not from the broker to market makers.
distractorExplanations.b: PFOF does not override best execution; the firm must still route for the most favorable terms reasonably available.
distractorExplanations.c: Commissions are charged to customers; PFOF is compensation the firm receives from execution venues for routing.

options.a: Publication of quotations for over-the-counter equity securities by broker-dealers
options.b: Continuing disclosure by municipal issuers that broker-dealers must review
options.c: Delivery of a preliminary prospectus to buyers 48 hours before confirmation
options.d: Net capital that broker-dealers must hold relative to aggregate indebtedness

distractorExplanations.b: Municipal continuing disclosure obligations for underwriters are SEC Rule 15c2-12, not Rule 15c2-11.
distractorExplanations.c: The 48-hour preliminary prospectus delivery for IPOs is SEC Rule 15c2-8, not Rule 15c2-11.
distractorExplanations.d: Net capital requirements are SEC Rule 15c3-1; Rule 15c2-11 governs publishing quotations for OTC securities.

options.a: Screen customers against SDN lists at onboarding and on annual reviews
options.b: Screen customers and transactions against SDN and blocked persons lists
options.c: Report blocked transactions to FinCEN on a SAR within 30 calendar days
options.d: Screen wire beneficiaries against SDN lists but not the account holders

distractorExplanations.a: Screening must cover transactions and list updates on an ongoing basis, not just onboarding plus an annual refresh.
distractorExplanations.c: Blocked or rejected transactions are reported to OFAC within 10 business days; SARs to FinCEN are a separate BSA filing.
distractorExplanations.d: OFAC compliance covers both customers and transactions; skipping account holders misses sanctioned account owners.

options.a: Retention of electronic communications for one year in any rewriteable electronic storage format
options.b: Backup on the firm email server, with deletion permitted after 90 days
options.c: Non-rewriteable, non-erasable format (or equivalent) for retained broker-dealer records
options.d: Retention of emails only, while instant messages and texts are excluded

distractorExplanations.a: Communications are kept at least three years under 17a-4(b)(4), in WORM or a compliant audit-trail system, not rewriteable storage.
distractorExplanations.b: Ordinary server backups with 90-day deletion fail both the three-year retention period and the 17a-4 format requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: 17a-4 covers business communications in any medium, including IMs, texts, and chats, as the SEC off-channel cases showed.

options.a: Gifts the firm pays its own employees as year-end awards above $100
options.b: Gifts from customers to representatives, capped at $25 per occasion
options.c: Salary and commissions the broker-dealer pays registered employees
options.d: Gifts and entertainment from non-customers that could impair objectivity

distractorExplanations.a: Rule 3220 targets gifts to persons employed by others in relation to their employer's business, not the firm's own employee awards.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no $25 per-occasion cap; the Rule 3220 limit is a per-person annual amount on gifts relating to the recipient employer's business.
distractorExplanations.c: Regular compensation paid by the employing firm is ordinary employment pay and falls outside the Rule 3220 gift limit.

series-99-readiness-check-regs-028.explanation: 3220 restricts non-cash compensation from vendors to associated persons. Gifts above the rule's annual per-person threshold are prohibited.

options.a: The broker-dealer or designated agent sending proxy materials
options.b: The issuer's transfer agent mailing ballots to each beneficial owner
options.c: The Depository Trust Company voting as the nominee holder of record
options.d: The broker voting on every proposal at its discretion after 10 days

distractorExplanations.b: Transfer agents deal with registered holders; street-name owners get materials through their broker or its agent.
distractorExplanations.c: DTC issues an omnibus proxy to its participants; it does not vote beneficial owners' shares itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Under NYSE Rule 452 brokers may vote uninstructed shares on routine matters only, not on every proposal.

series-99-readiness-check-regs-029.explanation: Beneficial owners receive voting instructions via broker; ops processes ballots and omnibus votes. The broker or its agent also records and submits customer voting instructions.

options.a: Duplicate statements sent to compliance, but no pre-clearance of personal trades
options.b: Pre-clearance of trades, restricted lists, and blackout periods around corporate actions
options.c: Disclosure of trades to the employer only for purchases of employer stock
options.d: Trading through the firm itself, with accounts at other firms left unreported

distractorExplanations.a: Duplicate statements are common, but ops staff with MNPI access are typically also subject to pre-clearance and restricted lists.
distractorExplanations.c: Policies cover reportable personal securities trades generally, not just purchases of employer stock.
distractorExplanations.d: Rule 3210 requires prior written consent from the employer for accounts held at other firms; they cannot go unreported.

options.a: Debits the customer's payable account and credits cash for the deposit
options.b: Debits cash/assets and credits the customer's receivable account
options.c: Debits cash/assets and credits the firm's commission revenue account
options.d: Debits cash/assets and credits the customer's liability (payable) account

distractorExplanations.a: This reverses the entry; incoming cash raises the asset (debit) and the amount owed to the customer (credit).
distractorExplanations.b: A receivable means the customer owes the firm, as with a margin debit; deposited cash is owed back to the customer.
distractorExplanations.c: Deposited customer cash is not revenue; it remains a liability until fees are actually earned and charged.

options.a: Positions, balances, transactions, and fees for the statement period accurately
options.b: Positions and balances, with transactions reported on the confirms instead
options.c: Transactions and fees, with positions shown on the annual Form 1099 instead
options.d: Positions at month-end, with fees disclosed only on the annual fee schedule

distractorExplanations.b: Confirmations are trade-by-trade notices under Rule 10b-10; Rule 2231 statements must still list account activity.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 1099 reports tax information and does not substitute for positions on a periodic account statement.
distractorExplanations.d: Fees charged during the period must appear on the statement; a separate fee schedule does not replace that disclosure.

options.a: Dividends and interest paid on covered securities during the year
options.b: Proceeds and basis for sales to assist customer tax reporting
options.c: Proceeds for sales, with basis left for the customer to compute
options.d: Year-end market value and basis of positions still held

distractorExplanations.a: Dividends and interest go on Forms 1099-DIV and 1099-INT; Form 1099-B reports proceeds and basis from sales.
distractorExplanations.c: For covered securities brokers must report adjusted basis; leaving basis to the customer describes noncovered lots.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 1099-B reports dispositions, not unrealized year-end holdings; unsold positions do not appear on it.

options.a: Customer cash awaiting investment in a bank sweep program
options.b: Unsettled customer trades awaiting T+1 settlement
options.c: Unidentified receipts or items pending proper allocation
options.d: Trade errors held until the firm absorbs the loss

distractorExplanations.a: Sweep balances are customer assets in a bank program, not unidentified items awaiting allocation.
distractorExplanations.b: Pending settlements are tracked in settlement or fail accounts; suspense is for items that cannot yet be identified.
distractorExplanations.d: Trade errors go to the error account; suspense holds unidentified receipts or unallocated items.

series-99-readiness-check-books-019.explanation: Suspense clears when research identifies correct booking; prolonged balances trigger audit flags. Items are later allocated to the correct customer or firm account.

options.a: Internal ledgers to DTC/depository records and counterparty statements
options.b: Customer statements to trade confirmations sent during the period
options.c: Internal ledgers to the firm's general ledger cash accounts only
options.d: Trader positions to their profit-and-loss reports for the day

distractorExplanations.b: Statement-versus-confirm checks are a customer communications review, not a books-to-depository position reconciliation.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash reconciliation is a separate control; position reconciliation compares security positions to DTC and counterparties.
distractorExplanations.d: P&L-versus-position checks are a desk risk control; operations position recon compares books to depository records.

options.a: Remaining margin debit after the receiving firm accepts the transfer
options.b: Remaining cash after securities transfer settles between firms
options.c: Remaining securities the receiving firm rejected as non-transferable
options.d: Remaining IRA balances moved by a 60-day indirect rollover check

distractorExplanations.a: A residual credit is money owed to the customer, not a margin debit the customer owes.
distractorExplanations.c: Non-transferable assets stay at the delivering firm or are liquidated on instruction; residual credit refers to trailing cash.
distractorExplanations.d: A 60-day indirect rollover is a tax distribution method, not the ACATS residual credit process between firms.

options.a: Recognition of tax gains when substantially identical securities are repurchased within 30 days
options.b: Recognition of tax losses when shares of a different issuer in the same industry are repurchased
options.c: Recognition of tax losses when substantially identical securities are repurchased within 30 days
options.d: Recognition of tax losses when substantially identical securities are repurchased within 90 days

distractorExplanations.a: The wash sale rule disallows losses only; gains are recognized normally even if the shares are bought back.
distractorExplanations.b: Only substantially identical securities trigger a wash sale; a different company in the same industry does not.
distractorExplanations.d: The wash sale window is 30 days before or after the sale (61 days in total), not 90 days.

series-99-readiness-check-books-023.explanation: Wash sales defer losses when replacement purchases occur in the 61-day window. The window runs 30 days before or after the sale.

options.a: Turning unclaimed property over to the SEC after dormancy periods lapse
options.b: Turning unclaimed property over to the state where the firm is incorporated
options.c: Moving dormant accounts into the firm's suspense account indefinitely
options.d: Turning unclaimed property over to the state after dormancy periods

distractorExplanations.a: Escheatment is governed by state unclaimed property laws; property goes to the states, not the SEC.
distractorExplanations.b: Priority goes to the state of the owner's last known address; the firm's state of incorporation is the secondary rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Dormant assets stay in the customer's name until escheated; suspense is for unidentified items, not long-term dormancy.

series-99-readiness-check-books-024.explanation: States claim abandoned property; firms must diligence and remit per escheat statutes. This is done per each state's unclaimed property laws.

options.a: The earliest purchased shares are deemed sold first for gain/loss calculation
options.b: The most recently purchased shares are deemed sold first for gain/loss calculation
options.c: The highest-cost shares are deemed sold first for gain/loss calculation
options.d: The average cost per share is used for gain/loss calculation

distractorExplanations.b: Most-recent-first is LIFO; FIFO relieves the earliest purchased lots first.
distractorExplanations.c: Highest-cost-first is HIFO, a tax-lot election the customer can choose, not FIFO.
distractorExplanations.d: Average cost is a separate method common for mutual fund shares; FIFO matches specific earliest lots.

options.a: Authorization from the receiving account owner and a matching entry
options.b: Authorization, matching debit/credit, and compliance review
options.c: A matching debit/credit, with authorization needed above $10,000
options.d: Supervisory approval in place of written customer authorization

distractorExplanations.a: The instruction must come from the owner of the account being debited (or lawful authority), not just the receiving owner.
distractorExplanations.c: Authorization is required for any inter-account journal; there is no dollar floor below which consent is waived.
distractorExplanations.d: A supervisor cannot substitute for the customer's instruction; journals between customer accounts require client authority.

series-99-readiness-check-books-026.explanation: Inter-account journals need client instruction or lawful authority and audit trail. These controls prevent unauthorized transfers between accounts.

options.a: Interest charged on the client's margin debit balance under its financing terms
options.b: Rebates paid to the client on cash collateral for its short positions
options.c: Costs or interest associated with securities borrow fails or settlement delays
options.d: Custody fees charged for safekeeping the client's fully paid securities

distractorExplanations.a: Margin interest is a financing charge on the debit balance, separate from borrow or settlement fail charges.
distractorExplanations.b: Short rebates are credits paid to the client on collateral, not charges arising from fails.
distractorExplanations.d: Safekeeping fees are custody service charges, not costs arising from borrow or settlement fails.

options.a: Produce requested records within 30 days of the examiner's written request
options.b: Produce requested records only after legal counsel completes privilege review
options.c: Produce firm-prepared summaries in place of the underlying source records
options.d: Produce requested records promptly in accessible form during examinations

distractorExplanations.a: Firms must furnish records promptly on request under 17a-4(j) and Rule 8210; there is no 30-day grace period.
distractorExplanations.b: Counsel may review for privilege, but production cannot be delayed past prompt; examiners are entitled to required records.
distractorExplanations.c: Examiners can demand the actual books and records, not summaries prepared by the firm.

options.a: Cash payable to the customer on demand from fully paid activity not yet withdrawn
options.b: Cash the customer owes the firm on a margin debit after a purchase
options.c: Cash in a short account held as collateral for the short position
options.d: Cash swept to an FDIC-insured bank deposit program and held off the firm's books

distractorExplanations.b: Money owed by the customer is a debit balance; a free credit is money the firm owes the customer.
distractorExplanations.c: Short sale proceeds held as collateral are not free; free credits are unencumbered and payable on demand.
distractorExplanations.d: Bank-swept cash is a deposit at a bank, not a free credit balance on the broker-dealer's books under Rule 15c3-3.

options.a: Share quantity and total cost basis by the split ratio, while leaving price unchanged
options.b: Share quantity and price history while preserving total market value per account
options.c: Per-share cost basis upward by the split ratio for each affected lot
options.d: Price history, with cash in lieu paid for each whole share received

distractorExplanations.a: Total cost basis stays the same in a split; only per-share basis and price are divided by the split ratio.
distractorExplanations.c: In a forward split per-share basis is divided by the ratio, not increased; total basis stays the same.
distractorExplanations.d: Cash in lieu is paid for fractional shares; whole split shares are credited to the account as shares.

options.a: Loss from price changes in the firm's proprietary trading inventory
options.b: Loss from a counterparty defaulting on its settlement obligations
options.c: Loss from being unable to fund settlements when cash is tied up
options.d: Loss from failed processes, people, systems, or external events

distractorExplanations.a: Price-driven losses on inventory are market risk, a separate category from operational risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Counterparty default is credit or settlement risk; operational risk is about processes, people, and systems.
distractorExplanations.c: A funding shortfall is liquidity risk, not operational risk from failed processes or systems.

options.a: Password reset followed immediately by large wire to a new external account
options.b: Customer naming a trusted contact person during an annual profile update
options.c: Large deposit from the customer's verified bank followed by a stock purchase
options.d: Customer switching from paper statements to e-delivery after several years

distractorExplanations.b: Adding a trusted contact under Rule 4512 is a protective step, not an account takeover signal.
distractorExplanations.c: Money flowing in from a verified bank into investments is ordinary activity; takeovers drain funds out to new payees.
distractorExplanations.d: A delivery preference change alone is minor; takeover patterns pair credential changes with outbound funds.

options.a: Clear exceptions below a set dollar threshold without investigating them
options.b: Investigate root cause, assign remediation, and escalate patterns per policy
options.c: Close each exception once the ops analyst marks it resolved in the system
options.d: Retain the reports for one year and review them at the annual audit

distractorExplanations.a: Small repeating exceptions can signal a systemic break; thresholds may prioritize review but do not waive it.
distractorExplanations.c: Supervisors must verify resolution themselves, not just rely on the analyst's own status flag.
distractorExplanations.d: Exception reports require timely review; deferring them to an annual audit lets breaks age.

options.a: Backup sites and data replication, with plan updates every three years
options.b: Data replication and recovery, with customer access deferred until systems return
options.c: Backup sites, data replication, and staffing for critical functions during disruptions
options.d: Backup sites and staffing, with the plan submitted to the SEC for approval before its use

distractorExplanations.a: Rule 4370 requires annual review and updates for material changes, not a three-year cycle.
distractorExplanations.b: Rule 4370 requires addressing how customers get prompt access to funds and securities during a disruption.
distractorExplanations.d: BCPs are kept by the firm and emergency contacts reported to FINRA; the SEC does not pre-approve plans.

options.a: The firm's proprietary inventory falls in value during a market decline
options.b: A customer fails to meet a margin call and the debit becomes unsecured
options.c: A system outage delays trade processing during the overnight settlement batch run
options.d: The firm cannot meet cash or securities settlement obligations on due dates

distractorExplanations.a: Price declines in inventory are market risk; liquidity risk is about meeting settlement and funding obligations when due.
distractorExplanations.b: An unsecured margin debit is customer credit risk, not the firm's ability to fund its settlements.
distractorExplanations.c: System outages are operational risk, even though they may later contribute to funding problems.

options.a: Updating to the most recent address and releasing pending wires
options.b: Enhanced due diligence and hold on disbursements until resolved
options.c: Immediate SAR filing before any contact with the customer
options.d: Closing the account and mailing assets to the newest address

distractorExplanations.a: Accepting the newest address without verification is the takeover pattern; resolve the conflict first.
distractorExplanations.c: A mismatch is a red flag to investigate; a SAR follows if the review finds suspicious activity, not as a reflex.
distractorExplanations.d: Closing and shipping assets to an unverified address compounds the risk; investigate and hold first.

options.a: Holding unallocated block trades until the adviser sends allocations
options.b: Absorbing losses on trades a customer later says they regret placing
options.c: Temporary posting of trade breaks or processing errors pending correction
options.d: Parking unidentified incoming cash until the remitter is identified

distractorExplanations.a: Unallocated blocks belong in an allocation or average-price account, not the error account.
distractorExplanations.b: A customer's regret over a correctly executed order is not a firm error and does not belong in the error account.
distractorExplanations.d: Unidentified receipts go to a suspense account; the error account is for trade and processing errors.

options.a: Longer settlement cycles that allow more time to match, affirm, and fund each trade
